response.consequence: With credential sync enabled, the Office365 calendar, Zoom, and other callers either throw "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" or store token data stripped of expiry fields. Token refresh then breaks or loops for synced credentials.
response.explanation: The keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` are evaluated as JS expressions. Each returns the string "[object Object]", so they do not mean "any key". The schema therefore requires a numeric property literally named "[object Object]", and the second computed key overwrites the first with an optional unknown. No real token response has that property. When credential sharing and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are both set, `minimumTokenResponseSchema.safeParse` either fails on the missing key or, because of the overwrite, ignores the number requirement entirely. The result depends on zod's handling of the duplicate key. The schema is also non-passthrough, so zod strips unknown keys such as refresh_token and expires_in from `data`. The comment says "any property with a number is the expiry" and "allow other properties", and the code does neither. The webhook secret check itself is safe, because APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED requires the secret to be set.
response.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses nonsensical computed keys, so synced token responses always fail validation

response.consequence: In credential-sync mode, refreshed credentials are returned with no expiry and a placeholder refresh token. Callers that save this data will have no expiry to compare against, and they will store the literal "refresh_token" in place of the real one. Integrations can stop refreshing correctly or become disconnected. I did not check the callers (Google, Office365, Salesforce).
response.explanation: `z.string().toString()` and `z.string().optional().toString()` both evaluate to the same string, "[object Object]", because zod types don't override `toString`. The two computed keys therefore collide, and the later one (`z.unknown().optional()`) overwrites the `z.number()` one. The resulting schema is `{access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown?}`. No "any numeric property is the expiry" check exists. Zod objects strip unknown keys by default and there is no `.passthrough()`. So for a response like `{access_token, refresh_token, expiry_date}` or `{access_token, expires_in}`, `safeParse` succeeds but returns `data` with only `access_token`. The expiry field and any real `refresh_token` are dropped. The code then sees `data.refresh_token` as falsy and sets it to the placeholder "refresh_token". The hypothesis said the parse would fail. It actually succeeds, but the data it returns is corrupt.
response.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses computed keys that collapse to "[object Object]" and strips the expiry and refresh token

response.consequence: No unauthenticated credential write was found in the unset-secret case.
response.explanation: packages/lib/constants.ts:103-104 defines APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED as CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY. The handler returns 403 before the header comparison unless both variables are set and non-empty. An unset secret therefore cannot produce an undefined === undefined match. The empty-string fallback for the decryption key is also unreachable, because the key must be set for the endpoint to run. The non-constant-time !== comparison is a minor hardening gap, not an exploitable bypass.
response.title: Unset-secret bypass is blocked by the APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED guard

response.consequence: After the first successful token refresh, every Google Calendar credential is rewritten in a corrupted shape. Later loads of that credential throw or can't authenticate, so calendar availability and bookings break until the user reconnects. The same stored-shape corruption is a persistence regression for existing credentials.
response.explanation: The old code assigned `googleCredentialSchema.parse(...)`, which returns the credential data. The new code assigns `parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema)`. That helper returns the `safeParse` result object, `{success: true, data: {...}}`, not the data. The wrapper is passed to `prisma.credential.update({data: {key}})` at lines 97-101. The persisted key becomes `{success, data: {access_token, refresh_token, ...}}`. The next `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` in `googleAuth` (line 75) then fails, or the credential has no top-level `refresh_token` or `access_token`.

other_findings.consequence: The connection still uses the old, possibly expired access token. jsforce may recover through its own refresh using the refresh token, but the freshly fetched token is discarded. There is also an extra token request each time the service is created.
other_findings.explanation: `getClient` refreshes the token and saves the new one to the DB. It then builds `jsforce.Connection` with `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url`, which are the old values. The refreshed `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token` is not used. The refresh also runs on every service construction, whether or not the token has expired.

response.consequence: With credential sync enabled, token refresh fails or corrupts stored credentials for Hubspot, Zoho CRM, Zoho Bigin and Google Calendar. The sync endpoint is called with no authentication, so anyone who can reach it can request tokens for a given user and app.
response.explanation: In sync mode refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw fetch Response without calling .json() or checking response.ok. The request carries only calcomUserId and appSlug, with no auth header or shared secret. Callers expect parsed token objects. Zoho CRM (zohocrm/lib/CalendarService.ts:217) reads `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error`, but a Response has no `.data`, so this throws a TypeError. Hubspot (hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts:192) reads `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` from the Response, which is undefined, so expiryDate becomes NaN. It then stores the Response object as the credential key and sets the access token to undefined. Zoho Bigin and Google use the same `.data` pattern. Non-OK responses are also passed through as if they were token responses.
response.title: Sync mode returns raw fetch Response, unauthenticated, unchecked; breaks callers

hypotheses.evidence_needed: Confirm whether APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED requires CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET to be set. Check whether the handler guards against an undefined secret or header. Check what symmetricDecrypt does with an empty key. Check whether any validation limits the keys payload shape.
hypotheses.failure_mode: The webhook compares the secret header with !== against process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET. If the env var is unset, a request that omits the header gives undefined === undefined, so the check passes and anyone can write credentials. The comparison is also not constant-time. In addition, the body parse (zod .parse), symmetricDecrypt and JSON.parse sit outside try/catch, so bad input gives a 500. The decryption key defaults to an empty string when CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY is unset.
hypotheses.investigation_rationale: This endpoint overwrites or creates a credential for any userId, so its authentication is the only protection. Check whether an unset secret or a missing header is rejected, and how the decryption key default behaves.
hypotheses.priority_rationale: An unauthenticated credential overwrite is account-level impact, and the endpoint is exposed publicly.

hypotheses.evidence_needed: Verify what the computed keys evaluate to. Run the schema mentally against a sample response of {access_token, expiry_date} or {access_token, expires_in}. Check whether the parsed output retains the expiry field. Check callers (Google, Office365, Salesforce) to see whether they save data containing the placeholder refresh_token.
hypotheses.failure_mode: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses computed keys [z.string().toString()], which evaluate to a fixed string key (the zod type's toString, i.e. "[object Object]"). The schema therefore requires a literal property with that name to be a number, and no real token response has one. In sync mode every refresh fails with 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned'. If it does pass, the schema strips unknown keys by default, so expiry_date and expires_in are dropped. The function also sets refresh_token to the literal placeholder "refresh_token" when it is missing, and callers may persist that.
hypotheses.investigation_rationale: The schema looks like it was written to mean 'any numeric property', which zod objects do not support. Check what the schema parses and what it returns.
hypotheses.priority_rationale: Every OAuth app refresh in credential-sync mode may be broken or may store corrupted tokens, which silently disconnects integrations.

hypotheses.evidence_needed: Check how the Hubspot (hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn), Zoho (zohoCrmTokenInfo.data), Zoho Bigin (tokenInfo.data) and Google (res?.data) callers use the return value. Check whether they call .json() on the Response. Check whether any auth is attached to the sync request.
hypotheses.failure_mode: In sync mode refreshOAuthTokens POSTs to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT with only calcomUserId and appSlug, with no authentication header or shared secret. It does not check response.ok. A non-OK or error response is handed to callers as if it were a token response. Callers that use axios-style (.data) or SDK return shapes (Hubspot, Zoho, Google) then break, because fetch Response objects have no .data.
hypotheses.investigation_rationale: The wrapper returns the raw fetch Response in sync mode, but several callers expect axios or SDK result shapes. Check each caller for compatibility.
hypotheses.priority_rationale: An unauthenticated sync endpoint can leak tokens. The shape mismatch breaks refresh for several apps in sync mode.

hypotheses.evidence_needed: Read createOAuthAppCredential for how teamId from the state is validated and whether admin access is always checked. Check which callbacks skip it (Google and Office365 calendar callbacks write credentials directly). Check handling of a malformed state.
hypotheses.failure_mode: OAuth state is passed as plain, unsigned JSON from req.query.state. The encode and decode functions are JSON.parse and JSON.stringify with no signature, nonce or session binding, so the state offers no CSRF protection. The state can carry teamId, so an attacker can choose which team a credential is created for. JSON.parse of a malformed state throws an unhandled exception in the callbacks. createOAuthAppCredential relies on throwIfNotHaveAdminAccessToTeam for authorization.
hypotheses.investigation_rationale: The state is attacker-controlled input that determines the target of credential creation. Check how the callbacks use it and whether team admin checks are enforced on every path.
hypotheses.priority_rationale: Possible CSRF-driven credential binding or team misattribution across about 12 OAuth integrations.
